rationale: B wins because it keeps the story where the facts can hold weight: 'Duolingo says beta users talked to its AI character for nine minutes at a stretch' is a clean behavior/data angle with the exact methodology questions a reporter will ask. A keeps reaching for architecture it has not proved, and 'Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence' is causality dressed up for a press release. A has useful proof lists, but B gives the founder sharper desks, cleaner constraints, and fewer fights with the facts.
gaps_in_A: 'Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence' implies a causal link the update does not supply. Growth and profitability can sit in the same paragraph without being married.
'pivoting from language app to AI learning platform' overstates the chess launch. One non-language course plus one AI language feature is a hypothesis, not a pivot.
'AI features become the primary monetization lever in consumer apps' imports a market thesis not present in the facts. That is a trend piece looking for evidence after the headline was written.

'Educators Say Duolingo Is Gamified Fluff. Its Users Are Spending Nine Minutes on AI Conversations.' uses engagement as rhetorical counterproof against a learning-quality critique. The set admits time spent is not learning outcomes, but the headline still tries to spend the same coin twice.
gaps_in_B: 'free beginner chess course' invents 'beginner.' The update says chess course, full stop.
'compute-heavy video feature' is a plausible inference, but still an inference. If margin risk is the money angle, get cost evidence before pitching it.
'the beta number is the first public engagement figure for it' adds 'first public' without support. Small phrase, big fact-check tripwire.
'the next earnings report is the natural follow-up moment' is a serviceable markets instinct, not a supplied peg. Keep it as follow-up planning, not part of the core why-now.
